Gentrification accelerated significantly after 2000, marking a sharp contrast to earlier decades. The rate of gentrification nearly doubled between the 1990s and the period following the 2000 Census [Source: ev-1]. Specifically, while only **9** percent of lower-income neighborhoods experienced gentrification during the **1990**, approximately **20** percent did so in the decade following **2000** [Source: ev-1]. Nationally, however, gentrification remained rare overall; since the **2000** Census, only **8** percent of all reviewed neighborhoods underwent this transformation [Source: ev-1].

The phenomenon was concentrated in specific metropolitan areas. Portland led with **58.1%** of eligible tracts gentrifying (**36** tracts), followed by Washington D.C. at **51.9%** (**54** tracts), Minneapolis at **50.6%** (**39** tracts), and Seattle at **50%** (where **7** out of **14** eligible tracts gentrified) [Source: ev-1]. In terms of raw numbers, New York had the highest count with **128** gentrified tracts [Source: ev-1]. Conversely, cities like Detroit saw only a **2.8%** rate (**7** tracts), while El Paso and Arlington experienced **0%** rates [Source: ev-1].

Demographically, gentrifying neighborhoods became whiter and more educated. Gentrifying census tracts recorded an average increase in their non-Hispanic white population share by **4.3** percentage points and a decrease in poverty rates by **0.7** percentage points [Source: ev-1]. In contrast, lower-income areas that did not gentrify saw their minority concentration rise (a **-5.0** change in white share) and poverty rates climb by **6.7** percentage points [Source: ev-1]. Educational attainment also shifted; urban residents now have bachelor’s degrees or higher at a rate of **35%**, compared to **31%** in suburbs and **19%** in rural counties [Source: ev-7], [Source: ev-11].

### Income Inequality
Income inequality has widened substantially across U.S. cities since 1980, driven by an economic shift from manufacturing to high-skill service sectors. Manufacturing employment peaked at **19.5** million jobs in **1979** but fell to under **11.5** million during the pandemic, while finance and professional services grew from **12** million to **32** million jobs [Source: ev-8], [Source: ev-11]. This shift concentrated wealth in large metros where white-collar industries thrive; between **1980** and recent years, nearly **80%** of the country’s population growth for those under **45** occurred in metro areas with over one million residents [Source: ev-8], [Source: ev-11].

National inequality metrics reflect this trend. The U.S. Gini coefficient reached record levels of **0.485** in **2018**, rising to **0.488** in **2020** and **0.494** in **2021** [Source: ev-3]. In specific cities, inequality is extreme. New York City has a Gini index of **0.5469**, significantly higher than the national average of roughly **0.40** recorded around **2013** [Source: ev-2], [Source: ev-11]. Other high-inequality metros include Atlanta (**0.57**) and Miami (**0.57**), while New Orleans reaches **0.56** [Source: ev-11].

The gap between top and bottom earners is vast. Using the 80/20 ratio (comparing incomes at the 80th percentile to those at the 20nd), New Orleans leads with a ratio of **7.87**, where the top earner makes $110,820 and the bottom earner makes just $14,078 [Source: ev-4], [Source: ev-11]. Boston follows closely with a ratio of **7.81** ($172,476 vs. $22,095) [Source: ev-4], [Source: ev-11]. Newark ranks third with a **6.80** ratio, Jersey City fourth at **6.09**, and New York sixth at approximately **5.8** [Source: ev-4]. The 95/20 ratio also highlights disparities; in Atlanta, the top earners make **17.5** times more than bottom earners, resulting in an overall metro ratio of roughly **18:1** [Source: ev-5], [Source: ev-11]. Between **2007** and **2014**, the national 95/20 rose from **8.5** to **9.3**, with inequality increasing significantly in **57** of the largest **100** metropolitan areas during that period [Source: ev-5], [Source: ev-11].

### Affordability
Housing affordability has deteriorated sharply as home prices have outpaced income growth for decades. Since **2000**, median household incomes grew by only **92%** (from $41,990 to $80,610), whereas median home prices nearly tripled, rising **177%** (from $122,775 to $339,937) [Source: ev-6]. On an inflation-adjusted basis, incomes increased just **8.5%**, while home prices rose more than **56%** [Source: ev-6]. By July **2024**, the Case-Shiller Index reached **325.78**, representing a **225%** increase since January **2000** [Source: ev-11].

This crisis is most severe in California and major coastal cities. Five of the six large U.S. cities with the highest price-to-income ratios are in California, including Los Angeles, San Jose, Long Beach, San Francisco, and San Diego, with ratios ranging from **9.6** to **12.2** [Source: ev-6], [Source: ev-11]. These figures are more than double the national average ratio of roughly **4.6** (or **4.7**) [Source: ev-6], [Source: ev-11]. Other expensive markets include New York City, Miami, and Boston [Source: ev-6]. In contrast, cities like Chesapeake, VA have a much lower 80/20 income multiplier of **3.8**, indicating relatively higher affordability for low-income earners relative to high-income ones [Source: ev-4].

### Displacement
Displacement resulting from gentrification is not uniform; it disproportionately affects minority communities due to racial stratification in housing markets. Research in Philadelphia indicates that residents moving from historically Black gentrifying neighborhoods tend to move to poorer, non-gentrifying areas within the city, whereas those moving from other gentrifying areas often relocate to wealthier neighborhoods or suburbs [Source: ev-9], [Source: ev-11]. This occurs because disadvantaged minorities face fewer affordable options and constraints such as discriminatory lending practices [Source: ev-9]. Consequently, while **53%** of urban counties are now majority nonwhite (up from a lower share in **2000**), white population shares have fallen by **7** points in urban cores since **2000**, compared to only a **3**-point drop in rural counties [Source: ev-7], [Source: ev-11].

Policies aimed at mitigating these effects include property tax relief for long-time homeowners and increased investment in non-gentrifying neighborhoods to ensure residential stability [Source: ev-9]. Without such interventions, the trajectory suggests continued polarization, as cities balance economic growth with the need for affordable housing and equitable development [Source: ev-11].
